feedback.problem:
For what reason does the function $f(x)$ given below have a discontinuity at $x=2?$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-2x+3, & x<2 \\ 2x-3, & x\ge 2\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's check the conditions necessary for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=2.$

- $f(2)=2(2)-3=1,$ so $f(2)$ exists. $✓$

- We calculate the one-sided limits and check if they coincide:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(-2x+3) \\  & =-2(2)+3 \\  & =-1, \\ {lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(2x-3) \\  & =2(2)-3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the one-sided limits exist but are not equal. Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ does not exist. $\times $ $\,\,\,$

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ has a discontinuity at $x=2$ because ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ does not exist.
